title: Chapter 10: RDS Proxy for SQL Server: Connection Management at Scale

questions.q: How does RDS Proxy for SQL Server authenticate to the database?
options: Through Secrets Manager only — IAM database authentication is not available for SQL Server through the proxy
Through IAM database authentication with 15-minute tokens
Through Windows (Kerberos/NTLM) authentication
With a hard-coded password in the proxy configuration
questions.explain: The chapter states RDS Proxy does not support IAM database authentication for the SQL Server engine — authentication goes through Secrets Manager, and Windows authentication is unsupported through the proxy.

questions.q: Which of these cause connection pinning on RDS Proxy for SQL Server?
options: Short transactions with parameterized queries
Read-only intent connection strings
Open transactions held across batches, temporary tables persisting across batches, session-level SET options, and MARS sessions
Using Encrypt=True in the connection string
questions.explain: The chapter lists the classic pinning causes: the proxy cannot multiplex safely when a session holds open transactions, cross-batch temp tables, untracked SET options, or MARS — pinning the client to a dedicated database connection.

questions.q: Which metric comparison tells you whether the proxy is actually multiplexing?
options: CPUUtilization vs FreeableMemory
QueryResponseTime vs WriteLatency
ClientConnections vs DatabaseConnections — if the two converge, the proxy is not multiplexing and something is pinning
DatabaseConnectionsCurrentlyBorrowed vs idle-client-timeout
questions.explain: The chapter says the ClientConnections-to-DatabaseConnections ratio is your multiplexing efficiency: hundreds of clients on dozens of database connections is healthy; convergence means pinning.

questions.q: How should you size the RDS Proxy pool?
options: Match the old direct-connection count exactly
Set it to the maximum allowed value for headroom
One database connection per application server
From the database's proven sustainable concurrency — slightly above active concurrency, with the proxy queueing the rest; oversizing reproduces THREADPOOL exhaustion
questions.explain: The chapter warns that sizing the proxy pool as large as the old direct-connection count defeats the purpose and reproduces the THREADPOOL exhaustion the proxy was meant to prevent; monitor ClientConnectionWaitTime as the scaling signal.

questions.q: During a Multi-AZ failover with RDS Proxy in the path, what do clients experience?
options: No interruption at all — queries continue mid-flight
A pause of a few seconds rather than errors, though in-flight transactions are still rolled back
The same 60–120 seconds of errors as without a proxy
Automatic replay of all in-flight transactions
questions.explain: The chapter explains the proxy re-establishes its smaller pool to the new primary so clients see a pause, not errors — but in-flight transactions are still rolled back and retry logic is still needed.
